sweep_summary: One bibliography item (Halle & Vergnaud 1987, An essay on stress): a secondary metrical-theory monograph that Glottolog files under mara1386; only archive.org controlled-lending copies exist (access-restricted, search-inside refused), so it was not read; low priority because it can only restate Tryon 1970. The important result of this search of works with stress in the title is a provenance error in the catalog record: the deciding quotation for Maranunggu ('5. STRESS GROUP (word).. bounded by juncture.. strong and weak variants.. phonological phrase.. 5.3 Three syllable words.. secondary stress optionally on the third syllable', locator 'Tryon 1970:14-15...') is verbatim from McElhanon 1970, Selepet Phonology, Pacific Linguistics B-14, pp. Tryon's Maranungku grammar is PL B-15; its entire stress statement is §1.5 p.10: 'Stress is non-phonemic in Maranungku, and falls on the first syllable of the word stem.. With words containing more than two syllables, a secondary stress falls on alternate syllables.' The catalog's fixed-strict initial + alternating coding therefore stands, but the quote, page numbers, the 'optional' trisyllable secondary and the phrase-level strong/weak overlay in the record belong to Selepet and must be replaced by Tryon 1970 §1.5 p.10 (DOI 10.15144/PL-B15). Ford 1998 (Emmi thesis, held by the project) gives the same initial + odd-syllable pattern for sister language Emmi but says nothing about Maranunggu stress.

new_statements.quote: 1.5 STRESS. Stress is non-phonemic in Maranungku, and falls on the first syllable of the word stem. Examples: /pán/, pan friend, mate; /tíralk/, tiralk saliva; /átyawa/, atyawa urine. With words containing more than two syllables, a secondary stress falls on alternate syllables. Examples: /mérəpèt/, merepet beard; /ŋúriñmìn/, ngurinymin blackhead.
new_statements.citation: Tryon, D.T. (1970). An Introduction to Maranungku (Northern Australia). Pacific Linguistics B-15. Canberra: ANU. §1.5 STRESS, p.10.
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary stress on the word stem, with secondary stress on alternate (odd-numbered) syllables in words of three or more syllables; stress is not contrastive. This is the only first-hand stress statement for Maranunggu and it supports the catalog's fixed-strict initial + alternating coding (10, 101, 1010..). It must REPLACE the catalog's current deciding quotation, which is verbatim McElhanon 1970 Selepet Phonology (PL B-14) pp. Note also that Tryon gives no 'optional' secondary in trisyllables and no phrase-level strong/weak overlay; those details in the catalog record are Selepet's, not Maranunggu's. Tryon's page 10 examples with 4 syllables (merepet is 3σ with secondary on σ3; ngurinymin 3σ) are consistent with 101; the record's 'domain_quote'/'domain_locator'/'notes' fields need rewriting to Tryon §1.5 p.10 and DOI 10.15144/PL-B15.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the record carries no classification quote; its domain quote and both locators (pp.14-15 §5; p.32 §12.3) and the volume number (PL B-14) belong to McElhanon 1970 Selepet Phonology, found verbatim in the sele1250 file we hold; nothing of it is in the held Tryon PL B-15. Tryon's real statement (§1.5 p.10, page image read) does support initial primary stress with alternating secondaries, so the stress class survives, but the record as written cites the wrong book and the wrong language for its only quotation and for domain=word (Tryon says 'word stem'). (2) Deciding source: Tryon 1970 short reference grammar via StressTyp2; per Ford 1998:31 it is the only published source on Marranunggu, and Tryon 1974 PL C-32 (held) adds nothing on stress, so the best published source is.
